tagline.text: A guitar-shaped, tranquil lake hidden in cloud-wrapped mountains

image.credit: Brenda Bonjoc / CC BY-SA 2.0 / Wikimedia Commons

items.credit: Selwyn Ken Abapo / CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: About 18km northeast of downtown Ormoc, this guitar-shaped volcanic lake sits some 650m above sea level in the Amandiwin mountain range. Paddle a kayak or bamboo raft across its calm, forest-ringed waters, then enjoy freshwater fish dishes at a floating hut on the shore while taking in the cool mountain air.
Lake Danao is a mountain lake about
18km
northeast of Ormoc, a port city on Leyte's west coast. Sitting at about

above sea level, it is cradled in the forests of the Amandiwin mountain range, which runs north-south through the middle of Leyte, and covers roughly 148 hectares. Seen from above, the lake narrows in the middle, giving it the shape of a guitar or violin — a hollow believed to have been formed by movement along the Philippine Fault and volcanic activity, later filled with water.
When it was first designated a national park in
, it was known as "Lake Imelda," named after the First Lady of the time, and a presidential proclamation in

renamed it Lake Danao Natural Park, as it is called today. The protected area, combining the lake and surrounding forest, covers about 2,193 hectares, and the lake also serves as a water source and irrigation supply for rice paddies in several towns across eastern Leyte. As a result, development along the shore is strictly limited, and tourist facilities remain modest, at the level of simple huts and a campground.

The lake's main appeal is its stillness. In the mornings, clouds resting on the mountainside settle over the water, and on windless days the forest is mirrored perfectly on the surface. Temperatures run a few degrees cooler than in the coastal city of Ormoc, staying pleasant even at midday and cool enough to need a jacket by sunset. Bamboo huts built on stilts line the shore, and renting a raft to head out to the middle of the lake for a meal and a nap is a classic weekend outing for locals.

This is less a sightseeing spot packed with attractions than a natural retreat for escaping the city heat. It suits travelers touring Leyte after crossing over by boat from Cebu, families based in Ormoc or Tacloban looking for a half-day outing, and anyone who enjoys lakeside camping and forest trekking.
The lake is calm enough for beginners to kayak with ease. Paddle past the narrow waist of the lake to the forest's edge on the far side, and human voices fade away, leaving only birdsong.

Roofed huts built on bamboo rafts, locally called balsa, can be rented by the hour. Loading up food and heading out onto the lake for a leisurely meal with family or friends is the signature way to enjoy the place.

Tilapia and catfish caught in the lake are cooked to order on the spot, grilled or made into sinigang, a sour soup. Under this paluto system — where you hand over the fish and choose how it's cooked — prices stay reasonable.
At sunrise, clouds drifting down from the mountains and mist rising off the water blanket the lake — the finest photo scene here. Only those who camp overnight or set out early get to see it.
Pitch a tent in the camping area designated by the park office and watch the stars. Temperatures drop noticeably at night, giving you a mountain night completely unlike the city.

blocks.title: A taste of the Leyte Mountain Trail

children.text: Opened in
, this roughly
40km

through-trail runs here from Lake Mahagnao to the south. The full route takes several days and is poorly maintained, but even a few hours on the forest trails around the lake with a guide is enough to feel the atmosphere of primeval forest.

The road up from Ormoc to the lake passes sugarcane and pineapple fields before gradually entering forest. With views opening up over Ormoc Bay and the plains along the way, the drive itself is an enjoyable part of the trip.

items.title: Day trip
items.subtitle: From Ormoc, half a day to a full day

children.text: Set out from downtown Ormoc by habal-habal or chartered vehicle, passing pineapple fields on the way up the mountain road
Arrive at the lake, pay the entrance fee at the park office, and take in the lake still wrapped in morning mist
Kayak or paddleboard a loop of the lake, out and back to the narrow waist section
Rent a floating hut and relax over a freshwater fish lunch out on the lake
Walk the lakeside forest trail, then head back down for sunset on Ormoc's seaside promenade
Arrive in Ormoc and pick up supplies, then head up to the lake in the afternoon to register for camping and pitch your tent
Dinner by the lake and stargazing — temperatures drop at night, so bring long sleeves
Photograph the mist and reflections at sunrise, then kayak on the quiet morning lake
Trek the forest trails around the lake with a guide
Head back down to Ormoc to catch a boat to Cebu, or continue on toward Tacloban or Palompon
Whether camping is available and how much it costs depend on park office policy, so it's best to check in advance with the Ormoc City tourism office or the park office.
Ormoc Airport has no scheduled passenger flights, so the usual route is to fly from Manila to Daniel Z. Romualdez Airport (TAC) in Tacloban. The flight takes about
1 hour 20 minutes
, with one-way fares around
. From the van terminal in downtown Tacloban, an air-conditioned van to Ormoc takes about
2 hours–2 hours 30 minutes
, for around
. Chartering a vehicle straight from Tacloban to the lake takes about
2 hours 30 minutes–3 hours
Coming from Cebu is the most convenient option. Fast craft such as OceanJet and SuperCat run several times a day from Cebu's Pier 1 to Ormoc, taking about
2 hours 40 minutes–3 hours
, with fares around
depending on seat class. Regular ferries that depart at night and arrive at dawn take about
5–6 hours
but are cheaper. Since schedules and fares change often, it's best to check the shipping line's latest notices.
Multicabs and jeepneys run from near Ormoc's public market to Lake Danao village (Barangay Lake Danao). The ride takes about
30–45 minutes
for around
, and it's a few minutes' walk from where you get off near the barangay hall to the lake. Rides back become scarce in the late afternoon, so be sure to ask about the last trip when you get off.
Habal-habal (motorbike taxi) round trip: about
, negotiate the waiting time in advance
Half-day taxi or van charter from Ormoc: about
, the most convenient option for a group
If driving yourself, most of the road is paved, but the last few km are narrow, winding mountain road that calls for slow driving.
Leyte has no clearly defined dry season, with rain falling fairly evenly year-round, but
February–May
sees relatively little rain and many clear days, making it the best time for a lake outing. Sitting at about
above sea level, the lake stays cooler than the coast, with daytime temperatures around
and readings dropping to around
at dawn and night.
From
June
, showers become more frequent, and in many years
October–December
brings typhoons and the northeast monsoon. Leyte has been hit hard by typhoons several times, including Typhoon Yolanda (Haiyan) in

, so during this period it's essential to check forecasts and build slack into your schedule in case boat services are canceled. Being in the mountains, roads get slippery after rain and clouds can easily obscure the lake views.

Around the lake there's little more than a campground and a few simple huts, so most travelers stay in downtown Ormoc and visit as a day trip. Ormoc is a compact city with its pier, market, and seaside promenade all close together, and business hotels running about
a night and mid-range hotels around

cluster near the pier and the city center. If you need to catch an early-morning boat, accommodation within walking distance of the pier is convenient. For camping, it's safest to bring your own tent and sleeping bag, and you should check with the park office in advance about availability and fees.

By the lake, tilapia, catfish, and carp caught there are served grilled, as sinigang, or cooked in coconut milk. Many visitors also buy food in town and lay it out at a floating hut. Ormoc is known for growing small, extra-sweet queen pineapples, and you can pick up freshly picked pineapple cheaply from roadside stalls along the way. In town, you can eat cheaply at seafood restaurants near the pier and barbecue stalls around the market, and it's worth trying binagol, a traditional Leyte snack of taro steamed in a coconut shell, or moron, a chocolate rice cake.
Mountain weather changes quickly — clear skies can turn cloudy and rainy within minutes. Bring an umbrella or raincoat and a light jacket.
The lake is most beautiful at
6–8 AM
, while mist still lingers. Clouds often cover the mountains by midday, so it's best to set out early.
There are no ATMs around the lake and card payments are rarely accepted. Prepare cash in Ormoc for the entrance fee, rentals, and meals.
If you go by public transport, check the last multicab's return time first, and if you're unsure, arrange a pickup time with a habal-habal driver.
The floating huts get crowded with local families on weekends and holidays. For a quieter visit, go on a weekday morning.
The lake is a protected water source, so you must carry out all your trash, and you shouldn't use detergent or soap in the water.

After crossing from Cebu to Ormoc and visiting Lake Danao, continuing on to Kalanggaman Island in Palompon or San Juanico Bridge in Tacloban lets you make a well-rounded loop of western and eastern Leyte.
Cell signal around the lake is weak or drops out in places. Save your driver's contact number and your accommodation's address in advance.
The lake is deep and cold, and there are no lifeguards on duty. Always wear a life vest when kayaking or rafting, and it's safest to swim only where permitted.
The forest trails around the lake and the Leyte Mountain Trail have poor signage and upkeep, making it easy to get lost. Always trek with a local guide and inform the park office of your route.
After rain, the mountain road and the dirt paths by the lake become very slippery. Sturdy-soled shoes are better than sandals.
When a typhoon or heavy rain is forecast, rockfalls on the mountain road and boat cancellations are common, so it's best to postpone your visit.
Entrance fees, camping rules, and operating hours can change based on the policies of Ormoc City and the park office, so check the latest notices.
Collecting plants or animals, hunting birds, and damaging trees are all prohibited within the protected area.

The longest bridge in the Philippines, linking Leyte and Samar, located in Tacloban about

A memorial park with statues commemorating MacArthur's landing, at Palo Beach south of Tacloban, about

from Ormoc by car.
Four islands off Inopacan on Leyte's west coast, known for beautiful coral reefs and white sand, about
